blogs.title: Hawaii, Reheated: The Ninth Circuit’s Broad Deference to Presidential Power Under §1182(f) Now Reaches Refugees
blogs.description: The panel leans heavily on Trump v. Hawaii to hold that the President likely has authority under 8 U.S.C. §1182(f) to suspend refugee admissions, declining any “searching inquiry” into the executive’s rationale. This post unpacks how the order treats refugees as just another “class of aliens” and what that means for the Refugee Act’s consultative architecture and annual admissions framework. It examines the doctrinal through-line from Hawaii, assesses whether any meaningful limits on §1182(f) remain when applied to USRAP, and anticipates how future litigation may test the intersection between §1182(f) and congressionally structured humanitarian programs.

blogs.title: Mandatory or Merely Authorized? The Panel Split on Whether §1522 Imposes Enforceable Duties to Serve Admitted Refugees
blogs.description: While the court stays the injunctions in most respects, it orders reinstatement of cooperative agreements to deliver “reception and placement” services, signaling that plaintiffs are likely to prevail on at least one APA claim grounded in 8 U.S.C. §1522. This post analyzes the majority’s signals that §1522 contains mandatory obligations—highlighting the repeated use of “shall,” specific duties for unaccompanied minors (§1522(d)(2)(B)) and for cash/medical support projects (§1522(e)(7)(A))—and contrasts them with Judge Lee’s dissent, which reads §1522 as largely permissive given its title and “is authorized” phrasing in subsections (b)–(e). It explores the stakes for APA §706(1) claims, the practical consequences for agencies that try to zero-out programs by terminating agreements, and how courts reconcile “shall” clauses that are conditioned by “to the extent of available appropriations.”

blogs.title: An Unusual Stay with Mandatory Relief: Appellate Tailoring, Nken’s Factors, and Refugee Services
blogs.description: The Ninth Circuit both stays the district court’s preliminary injunctions and simultaneously orders affirmative relief by directing the government to reinstate cooperative agreements necessary to provide §1522 services to already-admitted refugees. This post examines the appellate court’s power to craft partial, conditional stays under Nken, the vacatur of earlier carveouts and administrative stays, and the rejection as moot of the government’s emergency motion. It analyzes how the court balanced likelihood of success across distinct claims—presidential suspension of entries versus APA challenges to defunding—and the institutional implications of providing targeted, mandatory relief at the stay stage while the merits opinion is pending.

blogs.title: Appropriations as Constraint: Defunding USRAP, §1522’s ‘To the Extent of Available Appropriations,’ and the APA
blogs.description: The order flags Congress’s FY 2025 migration and refugee assistance appropriation and an $800 million rescission, then questions the Executive’s ability to halt services in the face of statutory duties. This post explores how appropriations law interacts with §1522’s mandatory language, whether an executive order can suspend funded programs absent statutory authorization, and the APA risks in terminating cooperative agreements without ensuring continuity of legally required services. It also addresses the interagency wrinkle—HHS’s statutory role under §1522 versus State’s historical use of cooperative agreements for reception and placement—and what the Ninth Circuit’s directive implies for future attempts to defund congressionally structured humanitarian programs.
